```{r setup}
`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) y else x

# For docx output: kable_styling with bootstrap_options produces HTML, which breaks docx.
# Override to strip bootstrap_options when rendering to Word.
if (requireNamespace("kableExtra", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tryCatch({
    to <- tryCatch(knitr::pandoc_to(), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(to)) to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
    if (!is.null(to) && to == "docx") {
      kable_styling_orig <- get("kable_styling", envir = asNamespace("kableExtra"))
      assignInNamespace("kable_styling", function(kbl, ...) {
        args <- list(...)
        args$bootstrap_options <- NULL
        do.call(kable_styling_orig, c(list(kbl), args))
      }, ns = "kableExtra")
    }
  }, error = function(e) invisible(NULL))
}

# Cousineau-Morey within-subject SE helper
# Args:
#   df          - data frame (one row per subject × cell)
#   value_col   - bare column name of the measurement (e.g. accuracy, rt)
#   subject_col - bare column name of subject ID
#   ...         - grouping variables for the summary (e.g. task, difficulty, effort)
# Returns a grouped tibble with columns: ..., mean_val, n, cm_se
calc_within_se <- function(df, value_col, subject_col, ...) {
  grp_vars   <- rlang::ensyms(...)
  val_sym    <- rlang::ensym(value_col)
  subj_sym   <- rlang::ensym(subject_col)

  grand_mean <- mean(df[[rlang::as_string(val_sym)]], na.rm = TRUE)

  df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!subj_sym) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(.subj_mean = mean(!!val_sym, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup() %>%
    dplyr::mutate(.norm = !!val_sym - .subj_mean + grand_mean) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!!grp_vars) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_val = mean(!!val_sym, na.rm = TRUE),
      n        = dplyr::n(),
      .cm_se_raw = sd(.norm, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
      M        = dplyr::n_distinct(interaction(!!!grp_vars)),
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      # Morey (2008) correction factor: sqrt(M / (M-1))
      cm_se = .cm_se_raw * sqrt(n / (n - 1)),
      cm_ci95 = 1.96 * cm_se
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(-.cm_se_raw, -M)
}

# Helper function to escape LaTeX special characters in captions
latex_escape <- function(text) {
  text <- gsub("\\\\", "\\\\textbackslash{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("([#$%&_{}])", "\\\\\\1", text)
  text <- gsub("~", "\\\\textasciitilde{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("\\^", "\\\\textasciicircum{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("$\approx$", "$\\\\approx$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("×", "$\\\\times$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("Δ", "$\\\\Delta$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("–", "--", text, fixed = TRUE)  # en dash
  text <- gsub("—", "---", text, fixed = TRUE)  # em dash
  text <- gsub("'", "`", text, fixed = TRUE)  # left single quote
  text <- gsub("'", "'", text, fixed = TRUE)  # right single quote
  text <- gsub('"', "``", text, fixed = TRUE)  # left double quote
  text <- gsub('"', "''", text, fixed = TRUE)  # right double quote
  return(text)
}

# Helper: figure path resolution
# Returns PNG for HTML output, PDF for DOCX output
fig_path <- function(fig_name) {
  # Get base name without extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(fig_name)
  
  # Detect output format - try multiple methods
  output_format <- NULL
  
  # Method 1: Check if we're rendering to LaTeX/PDF (most important for path resolution)
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    output_format <- "latex"
  }
  
  # Method 2: Check knitr's pandoc output format (most reliable)
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    pandoc_to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
    if (!is.null(pandoc_to)) {
      output_format <- pandoc_to
    }
  }
  
  # Method 3: Check if we're in a DOCX rendering context
  # Quarto sets this in the knitr options
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    # Check for DOCX-specific indicators
    docx_indicators <- c(
      knitr::opts_knit$get("quarto.document.format") == "docx",
      grepl("docx", knitr::opts_knit$get("out.format") %||% "", ignore.case = TRUE)
    )
    if (any(docx_indicators, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      output_format <- "docx"
    }
  }
  
  png_name <- paste0(base_name, ".png")
  pdf_name <- paste0(base_name, ".pdf")
  jpg_name <- paste0(base_name, ".jpg")
  
  # Find the actual file location
  png_abs <- NULL
  pdf_abs <- NULL
  jpg_abs <- NULL
  
  candidates_png <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", png_name)
  )
  
  candidates_pdf <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name)
  )
  
  candidates_jpg <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", jpg_name),
    file.path("output/figures", jpg_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", jpg_name)
  )
  
  for (path in candidates_png) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      png_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_pdf) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      pdf_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_jpg) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      jpg_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  # Choose format based on output type
  # For LaTeX: paths need to work for both R execution (with root.dir) and LaTeX compilation
  # Solution: return paths relative to root.dir for R validation, but use a wrapper in include_graphics
  # that handles LaTeX path conversion
  is_latex <- knitr::is_latex_output()
  
  if (exists("use_relative_paths") && use_relative_paths) {
    if (is_latex) {
      # LaTeX: return paths relative to reports/ directory (where LaTeX runs)
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name))
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", png_name))
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", jpg_name))
      }
    } else {
      # HTML/DOCX: Return relative paths from root.dir (which is set to project root)
      if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
        if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", pdf_name))
        } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", png_name))
        } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", jpg_name))
        }
      } else {
        # HTML: prefer PNG
        if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", png_name))
        } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", jpg_name))
        } else if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", pdf_name))
        }
      }
    }
  } else {
    # Return absolute paths when root.dir is not set
    if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(pdf_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(png_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(jpg_abs)
      }
    } else {
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(pdf_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(png_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(jpg_abs)
      }
    }
  }
  
  # Fallback: return relative path even if file doesn't exist (let LaTeX/Quarto handle error)
  warning("Figure not found: ", fig_name, " (checked: ", paste(c(candidates_pdf, candidates_png), collapse = ", "), ")")
  if (is_latex) {
    return(file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name))
  } else {
    return(file.path("output/figures", if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) pdf_name else png_name))
  }
}

# Wrapper for include_graphics that handles LaTeX path issues
include_graphics_safe <- function(fig_path_result) {
  # For LaTeX with root.dir set, fig_path() returns "../output/figures/..." 
  # which works for LaTeX but knitr::include_graphics() validates relative to root.dir
  # Use error=FALSE to skip validation since we know the file exists (we checked in fig_path)
  knitr::include_graphics(fig_path_result, error = FALSE)
}

# Helper: safe read
sread <- function(path) {
  # Ensure path is a single character string
  if (length(path) > 1) {
    path <- path[1]  # Take first if multiple
  }
  if (length(path) == 1 && is.character(path) && file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch(read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
  } else {
    NULL
  }
}

# Load pupil data for descriptives (if available)
# Try multiple possible locations for chapter 3 pupil data
pupil_data_paths <- c(
  file.path(proj_root, "data/pupil_processed/analysis_ready/ch3_triallevel.csv"),  # Primary location (from make_quick_share_v7.R)
  file.path(proj_root, "quick_share_v7/analysis_ready/ch3_triallevel.csv"),

  file.path(proj_root, "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_PUPIL.csv"),
  "data/pupil_processed/analysis_ready/ch3_triallevel.csv",  # Relative path

  "quick_share_v7/analysis/ch3_ddm_ready_with_auc.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_PUPIL.csv"
)

pupil_data <- NULL
for (path in pupil_data_paths) {
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch({
      pupil_data <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
      # Standardize column names
      if ("sub" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(subject_id = as.character(sub))
      }
      if ("effort" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>%
          mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
            effort == "High" ~ "High_40_MVC",
            effort == "Low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
            TRUE ~ as.character(effort)
          ))
      }
      # Map difficulty level from stimulus_intensity and isOddball
      if ("stimulus_intensity" %in% names(pupil_data) && "isOddball" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            isOddball == 0 | is.na(isOddball) | stimulus_intensity == 0 ~ "Standard",
            # Based on mapping: 0=Standard, 4=Easy, 3=Easy, 1-2=Hard
            stimulus_intensity == 4 ~ "Easy",
            stimulus_intensity == 3 ~ "Easy",
            stimulus_intensity %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Hard",
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          ))
      }
      # Map cognitive_auc column name (cog_auc_w3 for Chapter 3 primary, or cog_auc, or cognitive_auc)
      if ("cog_auc_w3" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"cognitive_auc" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        # Chapter 3 uses Decision-Phase AUC (W3.0) window (cog_auc_w3) as primary TEPR metric
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(cognitive_auc = cog_auc_w3)
      } else if ("cog_auc" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"cognitive_auc" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(cognitive_auc = cog_auc)
      }
      # Map baseline_B0 column name
      if ("baseline_B0_mean" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"baseline_B0" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(baseline_B0 = baseline_B0_mean)
      }
      # Data loaded successfully (diagnostic messages suppressed for rendering)
      break
    }, error = function(e) {
      # Error loading from this path, try next (messages suppressed for rendering)
      NULL
    })
  }
}

# Load behavioral data for descriptives (if available)
# Prefer bap_ddm_only_ready: has full Easy/Hard/Standard structure and matches DDM analysis.
# BEHAVIORAL_full lacks Easy trials; using it causes narrative/Figure 7 mismatch.
behavioral_data_paths <- c(
  file.path(proj_root, "data/analysis_ready/bap_ddm_only_ready.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL_full.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "data/analysis_ready/behavioral_data.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "data/raw/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "../bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
  "data/analysis_ready/bap_ddm_only_ready.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL_full.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/behavioral_data.csv"
)

behavioral_data <- NULL
for (path in behavioral_data_paths) {
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch({
      behavioral_data <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
      # Standardize column names
      if ("subject_id" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(sub = as.character(subject_id))
      }
      if ("task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(task = case_when(
            task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
            task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
          ))
      }
      if ("same_diff_resp_secs" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(rt = same_diff_resp_secs)
      } else if ("resp1RT" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(rt = resp1RT)
      }
      if ("resp_is_correct" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(iscorr = as.integer(resp_is_correct))
      }
      # Map effort_condition from grip_level
      if ("grip_level" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
            grip_level == "low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
            grip_level == "high" ~ "High_40_MVC",
            TRUE ~ as.character(grip_level)
          ))
      }
      # Map difficulty_level from stim_offset and stim_is_diff
      # Standard: stim_is_diff = FALSE or stim_offset = 0
      # Hard: Small offsets that are hard to distinguish from Standard
      #   ADT: 8 Hz and 16 Hz
      #   VDT: 0.06 and 0.12 contrast
      # Easy: Large offsets that are easy to distinguish from Standard
      #   ADT: 32 Hz and 64 Hz
      #   VDT: 0.24 and 0.48 contrast
      if ("stim_offset" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        # Ensure task column exists for mapping
        if (!"task" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
            mutate(task = case_when(
              task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
              task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
              TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
            ))
        }
        
        # Create task_type helper column for mapping
        if ("task" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- case_when(
            behavioral_data$task == "ADT" ~ "ADT",
            behavioral_data$task == "VDT" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ NA_character_
          )
        } else if ("task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- case_when(
            behavioral_data$task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
            behavioral_data$task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ NA_character_
          )
        } else {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- NA_character_
        }
        
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            # Standard trials
            stim_is_diff == FALSE | is.na(stim_offset) | stim_offset == 0 ~ "Standard",
            # ADT Easy: 32 or 64 Hz
            task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(32, 64) ~ "Easy",
            # ADT Hard: 8 or 16 Hz
            task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(8, 16) ~ "Hard",
            # VDT Easy: 0.24 or 0.48 contrast
            task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.24, 0.48) ~ "Easy",
            # VDT Hard: 0.06 or 0.12 contrast
            task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.06, 0.12) ~ "Hard",
            # Fallback: infer from magnitude if stim_is_diff is TRUE
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset >= 30 ~ "Easy",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset < 30 & stim_offset > 0 ~ "Hard",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset >= 0.2 ~ "Easy",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset < 0.2 & stim_offset > 0 ~ "Hard",
            # Default to Standard
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          )) %>%
          select(-task_type)  # Remove temporary column
      } else if ("stim_level_index" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        # Fallback: use stim_level_index if stim_offset not available
        # NOTE: Please confirm this mapping - typically: 0=Standard, 4=Easy, 2=Hard
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            stim_is_diff == FALSE | stim_level_index == 0 ~ "Standard",
            stim_level_index == 4 ~ "Easy",
            stim_level_index %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Hard",
            stim_level_index == 3 ~ "Easy",
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          ))
      }
      
      # Check if difficulty_level already exists but Easy trials are missing
      # If so, try to load from raw data file to get Easy trials
      if ("difficulty_level" %in% names(behavioral_data) && 
          !any(behavioral_data$difficulty_level == "Easy", na.rm = TRUE)) {
        # Try to load raw data file to get Easy trials
        raw_data_paths <- c(
          file.path(proj_root, "data/raw/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
          file.path(proj_root, "../bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
          "/Users/mohdasti/Documents/LC-BAP/BAP/Nov2025/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"
        )
        for (raw_path in raw_data_paths) {
          if (file.exists(raw_path)) {
            tryCatch({
              raw_data <- read_csv(raw_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
              # Check if raw data has Easy trials
              if ("stim_offset" %in% names(raw_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                # Map difficulty for raw data
                if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                    mutate(task = case_when(
                      task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                      task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                      TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
                    ))
                }
                if ("task" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data$task_type <- case_when(
                    raw_data$task == "ADT" ~ "ADT",
                    raw_data$task == "VDT" ~ "VDT",
                    TRUE ~ NA_character_
                  )
                } else if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data$task_type <- case_when(
                    raw_data$task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                    raw_data$task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                    TRUE ~ NA_character_
                  )
                } else {
                  raw_data$task_type <- NA_character_
                }
                raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                  mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
                    stim_is_diff == FALSE | is.na(stim_offset) | stim_offset == 0 ~ "Standard",
                    task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(32, 64) ~ "Easy",
                    task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(8, 16) ~ "Hard",
                    task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.24, 0.48) ~ "Easy",
                    task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.06, 0.12) ~ "Hard",
                    TRUE ~ "Standard"
                  )) %>%
                  select(-task_type)
                
                # If raw data has Easy trials, combine with processed data
                if (any(raw_data$difficulty_level == "Easy", na.rm = TRUE)) {
                  # Standardize column names to match behavioral_data
                  if ("subject_id" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>% mutate(sub = as.character(subject_id))
                  }
                  if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data) && !"task" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                      mutate(task = case_when(
                        task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                        task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                        TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
                      ))
                  }
                  if ("resp_is_correct" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>% mutate(accuracy = as.numeric(resp_is_correct))
                  }
                  if ("grip_level" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                      mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
                        grip_level == "low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
                        grip_level == "high" ~ "High_40_MVC",
                        TRUE ~ as.character(grip_level)
                      ))
                  }
                  
                  # Combine: keep all rows from processed data, add Easy trials from raw data
                  behavioral_data <- bind_rows(
                    behavioral_data,
                    raw_data %>% filter(difficulty_level == "Easy")
                  )
                  break
                }
              }
            }, error = function(e) {
              # Silently continue if raw data can't be loaded
            })
          }
        }
      }
      
      break
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("Error loading", path, ":", e$message, "\n")
      NULL
    })
  }
}

# Compute manipulation checks inline from behavioral_data when available (ensures fresh data on re-render)
if (!is.null(behavioral_data) && nrow(behavioral_data) > 0 &&
    requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("broom.mixed", quietly = TRUE)) {
  need_manip <- c("subject_id", "difficulty_level", "effort_condition")
  has_decision <- any(c("decision", "iscorr", "accuracy", "resp_is_correct") %in% names(behavioral_data))
  has_rt <- any(c("rt", "same_diff_resp_secs", "resp1RT") %in% names(behavioral_data))
  if (all(need_manip %in% names(behavioral_data)) && has_decision && has_rt) {
    dd_manip <- behavioral_data %>%
      mutate(
        decision = as.integer(if ("decision" %in% names(.)) decision else if ("iscorr" %in% names(.)) iscorr else if ("accuracy" %in% names(.)) accuracy else resp_is_correct),
        rt = as.numeric(if ("rt" %in% names(.)) rt else if ("same_diff_resp_secs" %in% names(.)) same_diff_resp_secs else resp1RT)
      ) %>%
      filter(difficulty_level %in% c("Easy", "Hard"), !is.na(decision), !is.na(rt), rt > 0)
    ulev <- unique(as.character(dd_manip$effort_condition))
    eff_ref <- ulev[grepl("Low|5", ulev, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
    eff_oth <- ulev[grepl("High|40", ulev, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
    if (is.na(eff_ref)) eff_ref <- ulev[1]
    if (is.na(eff_oth)) eff_oth <- ulev[ulev != eff_ref][1]
    dd_manip$effort_condition <- factor(dd_manip$effort_condition, levels = c(eff_ref, eff_oth))
    dd_manip$difficulty_level <- factor(dd_manip$difficulty_level, levels = c("Easy", "Hard"))
    dd_manip$subject_id <- factor(as.character(dd_manip$subject_id))
    if (nrow(dd_manip) > 100) {
      tryCatch({
        acc_fit <- lme4::glmer(decision ~ difficulty_level + effort_condition + (1 | subject_id),
          data = dd_manip, family = binomial())
        acc_glmm <- broom.mixed::tidy(acc_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.method = "Wald")
        rt_med <- dd_manip %>% group_by(subject_id, difficulty_level, effort_condition) %>%
          summarise(rt_med = median(rt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
        rt_fit <- lme4::lmer(rt_med ~ difficulty_level + effort_condition + (1 | subject_id), data = rt_med)
        rt_lmm <- broom.mixed::tidy(rt_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.method = "Wald")
      }, error = function(e) NULL)
    }
  }
}

  h1_row <- fl |>

  if (nrow(h1_row) == 1) {

    h1_beta_str  <- sprintf("$\\beta = %.2f$", h1_est)
    h1_cri_str   <- sprintf("95%% CrI $[%.2f,\\; %.2f]$", h1_lo, h1_hi)
    h1_p0_val    <- if (!is.na(h1_se) && h1_se > 0) pnorm(0, mean = h1_est, sd = h1_se) else NA_real_
    h1_p0_str    <- if (!is.na(h1_p0_val)) {
      if (h1_p0_val >= 0.999) "; $P(\\beta < 0) > .999$"
      else if (h1_p0_val <= 0.001) "; $P(\\beta < 0) < .001$"
      else sprintf("; $P(\\beta < 0) = %.2f$", h1_p0_val)
    } else ""
  }
}
```

\newpage

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

This chapter presents a hierarchical Wiener diffusion decision model (DDM) for a response-signal change-detection task in older adults. The primary model maps task difficulty to drift rate ($v$) and boundary separation ($a$), with starting-point bias ($z$) varying by task and effort but constant across difficulty levels (reflecting the randomized trial design). High-effort (40% MVC) conditions reliably reduced drift rate relative to Low-effort (5% MVC) conditions (`r h1_beta_str`; `r h1_cri_str`, where CrI = 95% credible interval; `r h1_p0_str`), consistent with degraded evidence accumulation under effort-induced arousal (H1 supported). No comparable evidence emerged for effort-related increases in boundary separation (H2) or shifts in starting-point bias (H4); posterior estimates were concentrated near zero with 95% CrIs spanning zero, though no formal equivalence was established. Non-decision time (H3) could not be directly tested in the primary model due to identifiability constraints in the response-signal design; an exploratory effort coefficient on $\log t_0$ was small and highly imprecise ($\hat{\beta} = 0.02$, 95% CrI $[-0.05, 0.09]$ on that scale), and no firm conclusion about peripheral slowing is warranted. Trial-wise pupil-linked arousal (TEPR) showed near-zero posterior associations with drift rate and starting-point bias; however, PSIS-LOO model comparison was unreliable (max Pareto-$k = 0.91$) and the TEPR measure likely conflates cognitive and motor-autonomic signals under dual-task conditions, limiting conclusions about pupil-parameter coupling. A supplementary interaction model (`pupil_scaled * difficulty`) explored whether arousal effects were conditional on task demands, as predicted by the Yerkes–Dodson law. All models converged satisfactorily. Overall, the evidence points most clearly to evidence accumulation quality as the primary locus of effort-induced interference in older adults; no comparably strong evidence emerged for shifts in decision caution or pre-stimulus bias, and measurement and design limitations prevent stronger claims about non-decision time and pupil-linked mechanisms. These findings advance our mechanistic understanding of how physiological demand affects cognitive aging, and demonstrate the utility of DDM decomposition for dissociating arousal-related costs across distinct stages of the decision process.

\newpage

# Introduction

## Age-Related Slowing and Strategic Adaptation

Older adults show pervasive response time slowing across virtually all task domains, a finding historically attributed to generalized processing speed decline [@birren1965age; @salthouse1985speed; @salthouse1996]. However, this slowing is partly strategic: older adults systematically widen their boundary separation — the amount of evidence required before committing to a response — to preserve accuracy under declining neural efficiency, favoring a cautious response mode over speed [@ratcliff2004aging; @starns2010; @rabbitt1979old]. Drift-diffusion modeling has formally documented this pattern: boundary separation ($a$) and non-decision time ($t_0$) are reliably elevated in older adults relative to younger adults, while drift rate ($v$) — the quality of evidence accumulation — is largely preserved in simple perceptual tasks such as brightness or letter discrimination [@ratcliff2001aging; @ratcliff2004aging; @ratcliff2008diffusion] but declines under more demanding conditions, including episodic memory retrieval and complex visual search [@spaniol2006; @madden1991]. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether physiological arousal state, independent of task complexity, can dynamically modulate these latent decision parameters within older adults.

## Drift-Diffusion Modeling of Decision-Making

The Drift Diffusion Model (DDM) formalizes decision-making as a noisy accumulation process: a decision variable drifts continuously from a starting point toward one of two response boundaries, driven by a deterministic signal (mean drift rate, $v$) corrupted by moment-to-moment Gaussian noise ($\sigma$) — the two opposing forces whose interplay produces the characteristic speed–accuracy tradeoff observed in behavioral data [@ratcliff1978theory]. This two-force description is the mechanistic core of the model, but it generates four empirically estimable latent parameters that jointly account for the full joint distribution of choices and response times: drift rate ($v$), reflecting the rate and quality of evidence accumulation; boundary separation ($a$), reflecting the amount of evidence required before committing to a response (response caution); starting-point bias ($z$), reflecting any a priori tendency to favor one response over another; and non-decision time ($t_0$), capturing perceptual encoding and motor execution processes that fall outside the decision process itself [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion; @voss2004interpreting]. The ability to decompose observed performance into these distinct parameters is what makes DDM particularly powerful for studying cognitive aging: changes in overall accuracy or RT may arise from multiple sources, and only the DDM can attribute them specifically to evidence quality ($v$), response caution ($a$), or peripheral processes ($t_0$).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ddm-process
#| fig-cap: "Drift Diffusion Model: Evidence Accumulation Process. Evidence accumulates from starting point ($z$) toward one of two boundaries: the upper boundary ('different' response) or the lower boundary ('same' response). Drift rate ($v$) reflects the quality of stimulus evidence; boundary separation ($a$) reflects response caution; non-decision time ($t_0$) captures perceptual encoding and motor execution. Total RT = decision time + $t_0$."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "70%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_ddm_process.pdf"))
```

In aging, DDM studies consistently show elevated $a$ and $t_0$ relative to younger adults, with drift rate $v$ largely preserved for simple perceptual tasks but declining under high cognitive demand [@ratcliff2004aging; @ratcliff2008diffusion; @spaniol2006]. An open question is whether drift rate and other decision parameters are further modulated by the organism's physiological arousal state. Answering this question has direct implications for theories of cognitive aging: if arousal selectively degrades drift rate, it would reveal that the neural efficiency costs of effort extend beyond peripheral fatigue to affect the quality of evidence accumulation itself — a finding that cannot be inferred from accuracy or RT alone. Conversely, if effort elevates boundary separation, it would suggest that older adults retain the capacity for arousal-driven strategic caution, informing rehabilitation and compensation strategies. The present study addresses this gap by combining a physiological arousal manipulation with DDM decomposition in a single older-adult sample.

## Arousal, Effort, and Decision Performance in Older Adults

The Yerkes–Dodson law [@yerkes1908] posits an inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance, with maximal performance at moderate arousal levels. Adaptive Gain Theory (AGT; @astonjones2005) provides a mechanistic, computational account of this relationship by linking the locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC-NE) neuromodulatory system to neural gain — the sharpness of signal-to-noise ratios in cortical processing. In AGT's phasic mode, characterized by moderate tonic LC activity, task-relevant stimuli evoke large, selective bursts of NE release that sharpen neural representations and promote focused, high-quality evidence accumulation. In the tonic mode, triggered by high and sustained arousal, NE release becomes tonically elevated and less stimulus-specific, increasing neural noise, broadening tuning curves, and degrading the fidelity of sensory representations — thereby impairing the quality of information available for decision-making. Within the framework of the Drift Diffusion Model, these mechanistic constructs map directly onto specific decision parameters: the quality of evidence accumulation described by AGT corresponds to drift rate ($v$), while the exploitation-versus-exploration tradeoff regulated by phasic LC-NE activation has been empirically linked to boundary separation ($a$), with phasic activation promoting strategic exploitation through wider, more cautious decision boundaries [@cavanagh2014]. When extended to aging, AGT predicts a leftward compression of the arousal–performance curve: older adults, whose LC-NE systems exhibit documented structural and functional decline [@mather2016; @huang2024], are expected to enter the performance-impairing tonic mode — in which drift rate ($v$) is degraded — at lower levels of objective physiological demand than younger adults. The present study provides an indirect test of this AGT-grounded framework by using isometric handgrip force as an effort-induced arousal manipulation and decomposing behavioral outcomes into DDM parameters that map onto the constructs AGT specifies.

The inverted-U framework and AGT, taken alone, are agnostic about age differences: they predict that all individuals show performance degradation at supra-optimal arousal, but do not specify where on the arousal axis that optimum falls or how it varies with age. An age-specific extension is required to generate predictions about older adults in particular. Theoretical accounts from [@mather2016] and [@huang2024] propose that aging compresses or left-shifts the arousal–performance curve, such that older adults reach the supra-optimal zone at lower levels of objective demand than younger adults would. This compression has been attributed to age-related decline in locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC-NE) gain modulation and reduced attentional filtering capacity, which together reduce the brain's ability to maintain an optimal arousal–performance operating point under increasing load — a mechanism elaborated in section1.4. Critically, it is this age-related compression, not the inverted-U per se, that licenses the prediction that a moderate effort level sufficient to engage younger adults may push older adults into a performance-impairing arousal state. Consistent with this compression hypothesis, several studies have documented that concurrent effort exacts a disproportionately larger performance and physiological cost in older adults than in younger adults.

Empirical evidence supports the view that concurrent effort is more costly for older than younger adults. Hess and Ennis [-@hess2012] found that older adults performing continuous arithmetic tasks exhibited significantly larger increases in systolic blood pressure than younger adults, with this physiological cost predicting greater subsequent fatigue. Similarly, Azer et al. [-@azer2023] demonstrated that maintaining a concurrent isometric handgrip selectively impaired older adults' accuracy on a visual working memory task with distractors, while younger adults were unaffected — consistent with age-related depletion of shared processing resources [@wickens2008; @verhaeghen2003].

The Yerkes–Dodson/AGT account and Resource Competition theory [@wickens2008] are not competing explanations but rather complementary accounts operating at different levels of description: AGT specifies the neuromodulatory mechanism by which arousal affects neural gain (and hence drift rate), while Resource Competition theory describes the functional consequence at the behavioral level — namely that shared cognitive resources, once depleted by a concurrent task, cause individuals to adopt more conservative response strategies. Together, they converge on the prediction that sustained physical effort should impair evidence quality while potentially increasing response caution. However, it remains unclear how these arousal-related costs decompose across the specific latent mechanisms of decision formation — evidence quality, response caution, and peripheral processes — particularly in older adults, for whom the capacity to compensate through elevated caution may itself be diminished.

## Pupillometry as an Index of Arousal

Pupillometry provides exactly such a physiological measure — pupil diameter tracks arousal state with high temporal resolution, serving as a non-invasive index of phasic arousal during cognitive tasks [@beatty1982; @kahneman1966]. Two components are theoretically relevant: baseline pupil diameter, reflecting tonic arousal and sustained alertness, and the task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) — a phasic arousal signal quantified here as the area under the curve (AUC) — which tracks moment-to-moment cognitive effort [@gilzenrat2010; @vangerven2004].

Cavanagh et al. [-@cavanagh2014] provided a key demonstration linking pupil-indexed arousal to DDM parameters. Using hierarchical Bayesian DDM in a probabilistic learning task, they found that pupil dilation specifically predicted increases in decision boundary ($a$) during high-conflict choices — interpreted as a phasic arousal signal prompting greater response caution. The present study builds on this approach but differs in three important respects: the participant population is older adults (vs. younger adults in Cavanagh et al.), the arousal manipulation is sustained physical effort via isometric grip force (vs. transient cognitive conflict), and the task is a change-detection discrimination paradigm (vs. probabilistic learning). These differences matter theoretically: if the arousal-DDM coupling found in younger adults under brief cognitive challenge replicates in older adults under sustained physical load, it would suggest that LC-NE-mediated gain modulation of decision parameters is a general mechanism spanning populations and arousal sources — not merely a task- or age-specific phenomenon.

### Hypotheses and Predictions

To test whether effort-induced physiological arousal modulates the latent parameters of perceptual decision-making in older adults, we manipulated arousal via isometric handgrip (Low: 5% MVC vs. High: 40% MVC) during a same-different change-detection task and decomposed behavioral outcomes into DDM parameters using hierarchical Bayesian inference. Based on the AGT-DDM framework and prior empirical evidence described above, we derived four directional a priori hypotheses. First, we predicted that drift rate ($v$) would decrease under High effort (40% MVC) relative to Low effort (5% MVC), reflecting degraded evidence accumulation due to resource competition or supra-optimal arousal. Second, we predicted that boundary separation ($a$) would increase under High effort, reflecting a compensatory widening of the decision criterion when evidence quality is degraded. This prediction draws on two converging accounts: @cavanagh2014 demonstrated that pupil-indexed phasic arousal during high-conflict choices predicted increased boundary separation in a probabilistic learning task, interpreted as arousal-driven adoption of a more cautious decision strategy; and Resource Competition theory [@wickens2008] holds that when shared cognitive resources are taxed by a concurrent task, individuals adopt more conservative response criteria to buffer against elevated error rates — a behavioral analog to boundary widening in the DDM (noting that Cavanagh et al. used transient cognitive conflict as the arousal manipulation, whereas the present study uses sustained physical effort, making the mechanistic bridge an extrapolation we address in the Discussion). Together, these accounts lead to the prediction that concurrent high-force grip should manifest as an increase in boundary separation relative to low-force grip. Third, we examined non-decision time ($t_0$) as an exploratory aim. Resource Competition theory predicts that maintaining a concurrent grip contraction occupies motor execution resources shared with the button-press response [@wickens2008], and prior dual-task research indicates that sustained manual force production can slow motor preparation and execution [@verhaeghen2003]. On these grounds, $t_0$ was expected to increase modestly under High effort, reflecting peripheral cognitive-motor interference rather than central evidence accumulation. This prediction is treated as exploratory — rather than a formal confirmatory hypothesis — because the response-signal design constrains how precisely $t_0$ can be separated from the task's fixed gating delay; estimation and interpretation limitations are detailed in Methods. Fourth, elevated physiological arousal induced by high-force grip was predicted to attenuate the pre-existing response bias, shifting starting-point bias ($z$) toward neutrality ($z \rightarrow 0.5$). Arousal has been theorized to promote signal-driven responding over heuristic-based responding by amplifying the relative weight of incoming stimulus evidence against prior response tendencies, and @degee2020pupil provided a DDM-specific demonstration of this effect, showing that phasic arousal indexed by trial-level pupil dilation reduced starting-point bias in a detection task. Because sustained grip at 40% MVC maintains elevated tonic arousal throughout the trial block — consistent with the tonic LC mode described by AGT [@astonjones2005] and with documented sympathetic and catecholaminergic effects of sustained isometric contraction at moderate-to-high force levels [@azer2023] — we predicted analogous criterion-resetting effects, while acknowledging that tonic versus phasic arousal may differentially engage this mechanism.

## The Present Study

Sustained isometric handgrip at moderate-to-high force levels (%MVC) is an established physiological arousal manipulation: contraction at intensities of 30–40% MVC reliably elevates heart rate, sympathetic nervous system activity, and catecholamine release, producing a broad state of physiological arousal that persists for the duration of the contraction [@azer2023; @wickens2008]. The present chapter applies hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion modeling to examine how physical effort (Low: 5% MVC vs. High: 40% MVC isometric handgrip) modulates latent decision parameters in older adults performing auditory and visual same-different discrimination tasks. Both sensory domains were included to assess whether effort-induced arousal effects on DDM parameters generalize across perceptual channels: if the pattern of results replicates across auditory frequency discrimination and visual contrast discrimination, this convergence is more consistent with a central neuromodulatory mechanism — such as LC-NE gain modulation — than with peripheral or modality-specific accounts (e.g., auditory fatigue or visual crowding). Both tasks also share well-characterized psychophysical properties that permit systematic manipulation of perceptual difficulty through stimulus offset magnitude, providing the parametric control over evidence quality that DDM estimation requires. Two factors were independently manipulated on every trial: **perceptual difficulty** (the physical magnitude of the stimulus offset — Easy, Hard, or Standard), which varied the quality of sensory evidence available for discrimination, and **physical effort** (the force level of a concurrent isometric handgrip — Low 5% MVC vs. High 40% MVC), which varied the physiological arousal state during evidence accumulation. These two factors are conceptually and operationally distinct: difficulty is a bottom-up perceptual manipulation, while effort is a top-down arousal manipulation. Trial-by-trial task-evoked pupil responses (TEPR) serve as an exploratory index of phasic arousal to test whether within-person arousal fluctuations predict changes in evidence accumulation or response bias. Together, these analyses test whether the characteristic slowing and cautiousness of older decision-makers reflect fixed capacity limits or physiological-state-dependent features modulated by effort-induced arousal.

```{r methods-demographics-inline}
    included <- read_csv(qa_inclusion_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

    demo <- read_csv(demo_path_ext, skip = 1, show_col_types = FALSE,
                     col_names = c('study', 'subject_id', 'subject_id2', 'demo_comments', 'completion',
                                  'bap_ses1_date', 'bap_ses2_date', 'bap_ses3_date', 'bap_ses_order',
                                  'bap_tablet_date', 'blank1', 'bam_ses1', 'bam_ses2', 'bam_ses3', 'bam_order',
                                  'bam_tablet', 'blank2', 'dob', 'age', 'sex', 'edu', 'hand', 'race',
                                  'ethnicity', 'first_lang', 'blank3', 'vision', 'prescription', 'blank4',
                                  'neuropsych_comments', 'adt_comments', 'vdt_comments', 'stx_comments',
                                  'future_contact', 'blank5', 'days_ses1_2', 'days_ses2_3'))
    demo_filtered <- demo %>%
      filter(subject_id %in% included_ids) %>%
      mutate(age = as.numeric(age)) %>%
      filter(!is.na(age))
    if (nrow(demo_filtered) > 0) {
      methods_age_mean <- round(mean(demo_filtered$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
      methods_age_sd <- round(sd(demo_filtered$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
      methods_n_sample <- nrow(demo_filtered)
      age_range <- range(demo_filtered$age, na.rm = TRUE)
      methods_age_range <- sprintf("%.0f–%.0f", age_range[1], age_range[2])
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    message("Demographics for Methods: using fallback values (69.5, 6.5)")
  })
}
```

# Methods

## Participants

Participants were recruited from communities surrounding the University of California, Riverside, through multiple channels including direct mail, posted flyers, social media advertisements, and word-of-mouth referrals. Eligibility criteria required participants to be aged 60–90 years, possess normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, demonstrate sufficient English language comprehension to follow experimental instructions, and exhibit right-hand dominance. Exclusion criteria comprised contraindications for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), current use of psychotropic medications, clinically significant neurological disorders, and major systemic health conditions including diabetes mellitus. 

Sixty-nine individuals initially enrolled in the study. Two participants were excluded following enrollment: one due to suspected mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and another due to possible essential tremor, yielding a final sample of `r methods_n_sample` older adults (age *M* = `r methods_age_mean` years, *SD* = `r methods_age_sd`, range = `r methods_age_range` years). Table 1 reports task-specific demographics (Auditory: *N* = 64; Visual: *N* = 65) for participants with usable data in each task. Three participants contributed data to only one task due to insufficient valid trial counts after applying the RT threshold and quality criteria (fewer than 100 analyzable trials in a given task), yielding N = 64 for ADT and N = 65 for VDT. Sample size was determined via a priori power analysis (G\*Power 3.1; [@faul2007g]). For a repeated-measures ANOVA with two within-subject conditions, medium effect size ($f = 0.25$), $\alpha = .05$, and power = .80, a minimum of 34 participants was required. The achieved sample of $N = 67$ exceeds this threshold by approximately 2$\times$ and is consistent with published hierarchical DDM studies reliably detecting group-level condition effects with $N = 30$–$60$ [@ratcliff2004aging; @wiecki2013hddm]. Twelve participants performed at or near chance level ($\leq$ 55% accuracy, compared to the 50% two-alternative forced-choice chance baseline) in some experimental conditions but were retained in analyses to maximize sample size, as hierarchical modeling approaches borrow statistical strength across participants to stabilize individual-level parameter estimates.

All participants provided written informed consent and received either course credit or monetary compensation for their participation. Study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of California, Riverside, and all experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with approved guidelines and regulations.

```{r}
# Function to calculate demographics for a dataset
calc_demographics <- function(data) {
  n <- nrow(data)
  
  # Age
  age_mean <- mean(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
  age_sd <- sd(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
  age_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', age_mean, age_sd)
  
  # Gender
  female_count <- sum(data$sex == 'female', na.rm = TRUE)
  female_pct <- round(100 * female_count / n, 1)
  gender_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', female_count, female_pct)
  
  # Education
  edu_mean <- mean(data$edu, na.rm = TRUE)
  edu_sd <- sd(data$edu, na.rm = TRUE)
  edu_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', edu_mean, edu_sd)
  
  # MoCA
  if ('moca' %in% names(data)) {
    moca_mean <- mean(data$moca, na.rm = TRUE)
    moca_sd <- sd(data$moca, na.rm = TRUE)
    moca_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', moca_mean, moca_sd)
  } else {
    moca_str <- 'N/A'
  }
  
  # Race categorization
  race_clean <- data$race
  has_white <- grepl('white', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE)
  has_black <- grepl('black|african', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE)
  has_asian <- grepl('^asian$|^asian,', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE) & !has_white
  has_other <- grepl('other', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE) & !has_white & !has_black & !has_asian
  
  race_cat <- rep(NA_character_, length(race_clean))
  race_cat[has_white] <- 'White/Caucasian'
  race_cat[has_black & !has_white] <- 'Black/African American'
  race_cat[has_asian & !has_white & !has_black] <- 'Asian'
  race_cat[has_other & !has_white & !has_black & !has_asian] <- 'Other'
  race_cat[is.na(race_clean)] <- NA_character_
  
  white_count <- sum(race_cat == 'White/Caucasian', na.rm = TRUE)
  white_pct <- round(100 * white_count / n, 1)
  white_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', white_count, white_pct)
  
  black_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Black/African American', na.rm = TRUE)
  black_pct <- round(100 * black_count / n, 1)
  black_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', black_count, black_pct)
  
  asian_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Asian', na.rm = TRUE)
  asian_pct <- round(100 * asian_count / n, 1)
  asian_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', asian_count, asian_pct)
  
  other_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Other', na.rm = TRUE)
  other_pct <- round(100 * other_count / n, 1)
  other_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', other_count, other_pct)
  
  # Hispanic/Latino - fix: exclude "Not Hispanic or Latino"
  hispanic_count <- sum(
    grepl('hispanic|latino', data$ethnicity, ignore.case = TRUE) & 
    !grepl('not hispanic|not latino', data$ethnicity, ignore.case = TRUE),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  hispanic_pct <- round(100 * hispanic_count / n, 1)
  hispanic_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', hispanic_count, hispanic_pct)
  
  return(list(
    n = n, age = age_str, gender = gender_str, edu = edu_str, moca = moca_str,
    white = white_str, black = black_str, asian = asian_str, other = other_str,
    hispanic = hispanic_str
  ))
}

vdt_stats <- calc_demographics(vdt_demo)
```

## Stimuli and Task Design

**Task overview** Participants completed two response-signal same/different discrimination tasks—an Auditory Detection Task (ADT) and a Visual Detection Task (VDT)—each performed under concurrent hand-grip effort manipulation. In both tasks, a standard and probe stimulus were presented in succession, and participants judged whether the stimuli were the same or different using button presses, followed by a confidence rating.

**Trial structure.** Both tasks shared the same response-signal timeline (see @fig-trial-structure). Each trial began with a jittered blank interval (1.5–4.5 s) displaying only a gray background. Participants were then shown a 3-second rectangular grip gauge with a marker positioned at either 5% or 40% from the bottom, indicating the target force level to be maintained using a hand-held dynamometer (left hand) at the corresponding percentage of their maximum voluntary contraction (MVC). MVC was determined during a brief calibration procedure prior to each task. Following the grip period, a 0.25-second blank screen and 0.5-second fixation dot preceded stimulus presentation.

**Auditory Detection Task (ADT).** The standard stimulus was a 0.1-second sinusoidal tone at 1000 Hz. After a 0.5-second inter-stimulus interval, the probe stimulus was presented as a 0.1-second tone that was either identical to the standard ($\Delta frequency$ = 0) or positively offset by $\Delta frequency \in \{8, 16, 32, 64\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. For drift-diffusion model (DDM) analyses, the four non-zero offsets were collapsed into two difficulty bins: Hard = {8, 16} Hz and Easy = {32, 64} Hz, with Standard = 0 Hz.

**Visual Detection Task (VDT).** The standard stimulus was a centrally presented sinusoidal Gabor patch (spatial frequency 1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, diameter 4°, duration 0.1 s). After a 0.5-second inter-stimulus interval, the probe stimulus was presented as a 0.1-second Gabor that was either identical to the standard ($\Delta contrast$ = 0) or showed a positive contrast increase of $\Delta contrast \in \{0.06, 0.12, 0.24, 0.48\}$, with all other parameters held constant. For DDM analyses, offsets were collapsed into Hard = {0.06, 0.12} and Easy = {0.24, 0.48}, with Standard = 0.

**Response collection.** Following stimulus offset, participants relaxed their grip and had a 3-second response window to indicate whether the two stimuli were the same or different using their right hand (index finger = "different"; middle finger = "same"). This was immediately followed by another 3-second window in which participants provided a confidence rating on a 4-point scale (1 = low confidence, 4 = high confidence).

**Trial counts and monitoring.** Each task comprised 150 trials distributed across five blocks of 30 trials each. Within each block, the five stimulus levels (Standard plus four offsets) were crossed with the two effort conditions (5% vs. 40% MVC) and presented in pseudorandom order with equal proportions (three repetitions per stimulus × effort combination). Hand-grip performance was monitored after each block, and participants received corrective feedback if they consistently failed to maintain the dynamometer at the designated force level (near the grip gauge marker) and/or for the correct duration (until offset of the probe stimulus).

## Equipment

The experimental task was programmed and executed on an Alienware laptop. Visual stimuli were presented via a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies, Montreal, Canada; 480 Hz refresh rate, 1920×1080 resolution) and viewed through a head coil-mounted mirror (viewing distance $\approx$ 12 cm). Auditory stimuli were delivered via MRI-safe earbuds (Newmatic Medical, Duluth, GA; 30 dB NRR). Behavioral responses were recorded using a RESPONSEpixx fiber-optic response box, hand-grip force via a MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs Inc., Philadelphia, USA; 100 Hz sampling), and pupil diameter via an MRI-compatible TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies, Montreal, Canada; 2000 Hz sampling). Stimuli were generated using Psychophysics Toolbox 3.0.18 [@brainard1997psychophysics; @kleiner2007s] in MATLAB R2022b (The MathWorks, Natick, MA). Data were collected inside an MRI scanner; neuroimaging results are reported elsewhere.

## Data Processing and Quality Control

**Reaction time definition.** In this response-signal design, reaction time (RT) was initially recorded as the latency from response-screen onset (“Same or Different?” prompt) to button press, termed **cue-locked RT**. However, perceptual evidence becomes available at probe onset (the second stimulus). To align RT with evidence accumulation onset, we derived **probe-onset-locked RT** by adding the fixed post-probe delay to cue-locked RT:

$$RT_{\text{probe-onset}} = RT_{\text{cue-locked}} + 0.35\text{ s}.$$ {#eq-probe}

where 0.35 s comprises 0.10 s probe duration plus 0.25 s grip-relaxation period. Probe-onset-locked RT served as the primary timing measure for DDM interpretation, as it aligns the decision process with evidence onset. Under this convention, the DDM non-decision time parameter ($t_0$) includes the fixed 0.35 s response-gating delay plus residual encoding and motor components. Cue-locked RT was retained for sensitivity analyses. This probe-onset-locked timing is our chosen convention to align $t_0$ with evidence onset; some DDM studies alternatively use cue-locked or response-locked reference points depending on task structure.

**Trial exclusion criteria.** To minimize the influence of premature or accidental button presses, trials with cue-locked RT < 0.20 s were excluded from the primary analysis. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using alternative cutoffs of 0.15 s and 0.25 s. Additional exclusions included missed responses, invalid run performance, and trials with non-positive or missing RT values. The same exclusion criteria were applied to both cue-locked and probe-onset-locked RT datasets (which differ only by the fixed 0.35 s offset). For pupil-linked DDM models, trials additionally required valid pupil data (see Pupillometry Preprocessing section). These steps are described above.

## Experimental Design and Statistical Modeling

**Design.** The study employed a 2 (Task: ADT, VDT) × 3 (Difficulty: Standard, Easy, Hard) × 2 (Effort: Low, High) within-subjects factorial design, yielding 12 experimental conditions per participant. Because difficulty is determined by stimulus offset magnitude and thus unknown at trial onset, it was not included as a predictor of starting-point bias in the primary DDM specification.

**Modeling approach.** ADT and VDT were modeled *jointly* in a single hierarchical Bayesian DDM, with Task (ADT vs. VDT) included as a fixed effect on starting-point bias $z$. This joint specification estimates task-specific parameter offsets (i.e., how ADT and VDT differ in bias) while sharing subject-level random-effect variance across tasks, allowing hierarchical shrinkage to stabilize individual-level estimates. Importantly, drift rate $v$ and boundary separation $a$ were not modeled as functions of Task in the primary model — instead, task-specific estimates for these parameters are provided as a sensitivity analysis in Appendix A4.3. This choice reflects our primary interest in the pooled effort and difficulty effects, with task-modality differences treated as secondary context.

## Statistical Analysis Overview {#sec-stats-overview}

Analyses proceeded in three stages. First, **manipulation checks** confirmed that difficulty and effort affected behavioral performance (accuracy and RT) as intended, using generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMM, binomial family) for accuracy and linear mixed-effects models (LMM) for median RT, each with fixed effects for Difficulty, Effort, and Task and random intercepts for participant; these results are reported in Appendix A7. Second, the **primary DDM analysis** used a hierarchical Bayesian Wiener diffusion model fit via `brms` [@burkner2017brms] in R [@R], with model comparison via Pareto-smoothed importance sampling LOO cross-validation (PSIS-LOO; [@vehtari2017loo]); full model specification is described in @sec-ddm-spec. Third, **pupil-linked DDM extensions** tested whether trial-wise task-evoked pupil responses (TEPR) modulated drift rate or response bias, using a nested sequence of pupil-augmented models compared via PSIS-LOO (@sec-pupil-ddm-models). Sensitivity analyses across RT cutoff thresholds are reported in Appendix A4.2.

## Pupillometry Preprocessing and AUC Features {#sec-pupil-preprocessing}

**Recording and hardware.** Pupil diameter was continuously recorded using an MRI-compatible TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies, Montreal, Canada) sampling at 2000 Hz. Raw eye-tracking data were exported as .mat files and processed through a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline designed to ensure high-quality pupillometry measurements.

**Artifact correction and quality control.** Blink artifacts and invalid samples were removed using the ET-remove-artifacts MATLAB toolbox (Huang et al., 2020), which employs a velocity-based detection algorithm configured with a 100th-order low-pass filter (passband: 10 Hz, stopband: 12 Hz) and peak/trough threshold factors of 5 standard deviations above baseline. Artifacts exceeding 2 seconds in duration were replaced with missing values rather than interpolated, following best practices for handling extended periods of signal loss. All recordings then underwent manual inspection using the toolbox's interactive plot editor to identify and correct any remaining undetected artifacts.

**Trial alignment and downsampling.** Cleaned pupil data were trial-aligned using event timestamps synchronized with behavioral event markers, then downsampled from 2000 Hz to 250 Hz using an 8th-order anti-aliasing filter to preserve signal quality while reducing computational demands. Baseline correction was applied by subtracting the mean pupil diameter during the baseline window (-0.5 s to 0 s relative to squeeze onset) from all timepoints in the trial.

**Decision-Phase AUC (W3.0) and rationale.** We computed trial-wise cognitive AUC from baseline-corrected pupil diameter in a window anchored to **probe onset** (the second stimulus; evidence onset). The primary AUC window — hereafter the *Decision-Phase AUC* (W3.0) — is a 3.0-s window spanning probe + 0.3 s to probe + 3.3 s (4.65 s to 7.65 s relative to squeeze onset), using trapezoidal integration. The +0.3 s offset accounts for pupil latency, and the 3.0 s duration captures the bulk of the task-evoked pupil response (TEPR), which peaks at ~2.95 s after probe onset. Because the response prompt occurs 0.35 s after probe onset, most of the TEPR unfolds during the response period; accordingly, the Decision-Phase AUC should be interpreted as TEPR magnitude during decision/response rather than a strictly pre-response predictor. Notably, because the response prompt appeared at probe-onset + 0.35 s and mean response times were approximately 0.6 s (cue-locked), the Decision-Phase AUC window captures both pre-response (phasic arousal during evidence accumulation) and post-response (motor execution, decision confidence, post-decisional processing) pupil dynamics. To control for this, RT was included as a covariate in all pupil-DDM models (@sec-pupil-ddm-models).

@fig-auc-timeline shows the response-signal timing structure used in analyses.

```{r}
#| label: fig-auc-timeline
#| fig-cap: "Response-signal timing used in analyses. Probe onset (2nd stimulus; evidence onset) precedes the response prompt by a fixed 0.35 s; Decision-Phase AUC (W3.0) is probe-anchored."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "70%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("AUC_timeline_v2.png"))
```

**Confounds and sensitivity checks.** Because pupil diameter is sensitive to luminance, autonomic balance, and motor activity in addition to arousal [@beatty1982; @loewenfeld1999], TEPR is interpreted in this study as a relative index of phasic arousal [@beatty1982; @gilzenrat2010] within our controlled MRI environment — we acknowledge that TEPR reflects a mixture of cognitive, autonomic, and motor-related pupil dynamics (see Discussion for limitations of this interpretation). We addressed potential post-response and motor confounds through multiple approaches. In trial-level pupil–DDM coupling models, RT was included as a covariate to control for decision state and prevent RT-driven pupil confounds. We also defined an optional motor-buffered variant of the Decision-Phase AUC (W3.0) that truncates the window 150 ms before the button press ($t_{\mathrm{resp}} - 0.15\,\mathrm{s}$); these buffered AUCs require re-processing the flat files with RT-aligned pupil traces and were computed for sensitivity analyses. Primary analyses use the Decision-Phase AUC (W3.0).

## DDM Overview and Parameter Definitions

The DDM framework and its four parameters ($v$, $a$, $z$, $t_0$) are introduced in Section 1.2; this section describes the implementation-specific decisions for the present study.

## Decision Coding and Parameterization

**Response-side coding rationale.** We employed **response-side coding** (also called "stimulus coding" or "response coding") where the upper boundary corresponds to "different" responses and the lower boundary to "same" responses (see @fig-ddm-process), rather than accuracy-based coding where boundaries represent correct/incorrect responses. This specification is necessary to disentangle *response bias* (a preference for one response alternative regardless of stimulus truth) from *discriminability* (drift rate) [@wiecki2013hddm; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. In accuracy-based coding, bias would imply a preference for being correct (which is conceptually trivial), whereas response-side coding allows us to model the meaningful response preference for the "same" option commonly observed in detection tasks. This is particularly important for same/different discrimination where participants often exhibit response-specific biases (e.g., a conservative "same" bias) rather than general accuracy biases. Previous work has demonstrated that phasic arousal reduces such response biases in detection tasks [@degee2020pupil], and capturing this effect requires mapping boundaries to response alternatives.

**Implementation and model leverage.** Response-side coding was implemented by creating a binary response indicator, coded as 1 for "different" responses and 0 for "same" responses, ensuring accurate mapping to DDM boundary assignments. Standard (Δ=0) trials provide critical leverage for identifying bias under this coding scheme, as they isolate response preference from evidence strength; descriptive choice proportions and model-implied patterns are reported in Results. Crucially, the data were modeled using Stimulus/Response coding via the `dec(response)` argument, where the upper boundary represents a "Different" response and the lower boundary represents a "Same" response. Accuracy coding (Correct vs. Incorrect) was intentionally avoided. Response coding uniquely allows the model to estimate true pre-stimulus starting-point bias ($z$) toward a specific physical response—a critical strategic shift often observed in cognitive aging. Because of this parameterization, accurate evidence accumulation for "Standard" (Same) trials is mathematically represented as a negative drift rate (moving toward the lower boundary), rather than a deficit in processing.

Full link function specifications and the Wiener likelihood are provided in Appendix A6.

## Model Specification: Standard-only Calibration and Primary Model {#sec-ddm-spec}

**Standard-only bias calibration model.** To isolate starting-point bias from drift-rate estimation, we first fit a hierarchical Wiener DDM to Standard trials only (~3.6k trials under the primary filter). Starting-point bias ($z$) was allowed to vary by Task and Effort (known pre-trial) but constrained to be constant across Difficulty levels, as trial difficulty was randomized and unknown at decision onset. Full brms formula syntax is provided in Appendix A6.

**Primary analysis model (behavioral DDM; no pupil).** Drift rate ($v$) and boundary separation ($a$) were each modeled as additive functions of difficulty (treatment-coded, Standard as reference) and effort condition (treatment-coded, Low as reference). Starting-point bias ($z$) was modeled as a function of task and effort but not difficulty, because trial difficulty is randomized and unknown before evidence accumulation begins [@fig-model-matrix]. Non-decision time ($t_0$) was constrained to an intercept-only specification based on pilot analyses indicating poor identification of condition-specific estimates in the response-signal paradigm (see Results Section 3.5 for justification). Random intercepts by participant were included for $v$, $a$, and $z$; $t_0$ was modeled as fixed-only to improve identifiability. Full brms formula syntax and hierarchical model structure are provided in Appendix A6.

**RT timing convention.** RT was defined as the latency from response-screen onset to button press; probe-onset-locked RT was derived by adding the fixed 0.35-s post-probe delay to cue-locked RT, so that the accumulation window aligns with evidence onset at the probe stimulus. Probe-onset-locked RT was selected as the primary timing convention as it aligns non-decision time ($t_0$) with the onset of evidence accumulation at the probe stimulus. The expected 0.35-s rightward shift of the probe-onset distribution relative to cue-locked RT (@fig-rt-distributions) validates correct implementation of the timing transformation.

Sensitivity analyses using cue-locked RT and alternative lower-bound cutoffs (0.15 s and 0.25 s) are reported in Appendix A4.

@fig-model-matrix provides a visual summary of how experimental predictors map onto each DDM parameter in the primary model, highlighting the key constraint that starting-point bias ($z$) does not vary by difficulty because trial difficulty is randomized and unknown before evidence accumulation begins.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model-matrix
#| fig-cap: "Predictor-to-parameter mapping for the primary DDM. Checkmarks indicate included predictors; dashes indicate excluded predictors. Difficulty is excluded from the bias formula because trial difficulty is randomized and unknown at decision onset, preventing participants from adjusting their starting point based on difficulty. Task and Effort are included in bias because these conditions are known pre-stimulus. Complete brms formulas are shown for each parameter."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: "htbp"
#| out-width: "70%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("matrix.png"))
```

To confirm that the difficulty and effort manipulations affected behavioral performance as intended — independent of DDM assumptions — we conducted mixed-effects models for accuracy (GLMM, binomial) and median reaction time (LMM), each including fixed effects for difficulty, effort, and task, with random intercepts for participant. Analyses were restricted to Easy and Hard trials; full model details and results are reported in Appendix A7.

## Pupil-Linked DDM Extensions {#sec-pupil-ddm-models}

**Pupil-linked DDM extensions (trial-level phasic arousal).** To test whether momentary arousal modulates evidence accumulation or response bias, we extended the behavioral DDM by adding a trial-level pupil predictor interpreted as an index of phasic arousal. The primary pupil metric was a cleaned, baseline-corrected, and participant-standardized response (interpreted here as a phasic arousal signal) summarized per trial and z-scored within participant (`pupil_scaled`). We evaluated a nested sequence of pupil-linked models: (i) behavioral baseline (no pupil predictor), (ii) pupil predicting starting-point bias, and (iii) pupil predicting both drift and bias. Competing pupil models were compared using Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS‑LOO; an efficient approximation to standard LOO-CV), and inference focused on posterior distributions of pupil coefficients on the link scale as well as condition-level posterior predictions. Results from these pupil-linked models are reported in the Results section.

**Pupil × Difficulty interaction model.** To evaluate the Yerkes–Dodson prediction that arousal effects on decision-making should diverge by difficulty — with optimal arousal shifting as a function of task demands — `pupil_scaled` was additionally entered as an interaction with task `difficulty` for both drift rate ($v$) and boundary separation ($a$): `pupil_scaled * difficulty_3`. This specification allows the model to test whether momentary arousal differentially predicts evidence accumulation across difficulty levels — for example, providing a performance boost on Easy trials (where arousal may elevate an already positive drift) while causing overload on Hard or Standard trials (where supra-optimal arousal may further degrade a low or negative drift). Subject-level variability in the arousal–difficulty coupling was captured by including the full interaction in the random-effects structure: `(1 + pupil_scaled * difficulty_3 | subject_id)`. Non-decision time and starting-point bias formulas were held constant across difficulty, consistent with the primary model.

## Priors, Computation, and Diagnostics {#sec-ddm-priors}

Priors were weakly informative and specified on the link scale. The boundary separation intercept used $\mathcal{N}(\log 1.3,\; 0.25)$ (corresponding to $a \approx 1.3$ at baseline), the non-decision time intercept used $\mathcal{N}(\log 0.35,\; 0.15)$ ($t_0 \approx 0.35$ s, probe-onset-locked), the drift rate intercept used $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, and the starting-point bias intercept used $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$ ($z \approx 0.5$, no bias). Full prior specifications for slopes and random effects are provided in Appendix A6.

Convergence was assessed using $\hat{R} < 1.01$ and minimum bulk ESS $> 400$; all reported models satisfied these criteria. Model comparison used Pareto-smoothed importance sampling LOO cross-validation (PSIS-LOO; @vehtari2017loo), with ELPD differences exceeding 4 considered meaningful; results are in Section 3.3.

Model fit was evaluated using posterior predictive checks (PPC), including subject-level quantile-probability plots, Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics, and residual heatmaps (full PPC diagnostics in Appendix A3). PPC deviations in fast-tail regions — a known limitation of standard Wiener DDM — did not affect inference on key parameter contrasts.
